prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout with one person immediately in front of the camera wearer, roughly 0.3–0.8 m away, and another person partly visible along the left edge at about 1–2 m; the nearby person is much closer than the ground, parked vehicles, and other background surfaces. Across frames 1–4, the central person remains within or near the camera wearer’s arm’s reach, with the face and upper torso nearest and the arms extending downward toward the bottom edge; in frame 5 the person shifts toward the right and appears slightly farther or more obliquely oriented. The left person stays separated from the central person by roughly 0.5–1.5 m and is partly occluded or cropped, while the motorcycle/car region lies behind and to the right of the people. Compared with RGB, the map makes foreground–background separation and the extreme closeness of the central person clearer, but it is unreliable for exact metric distances, merges some adjacent body and ground regions, and loses fine object boundaries.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently identifies two people: one partly cropped on the left and one large person directly in front of the camera wearer, with the central person occupying most of the foreground and therefore likely within about 0.3–0.8 m. It also isolates a tie-like region on the central person in frame 1, a car at the upper-right edge in frames 1, 3, and 5, and a motorcycle to the right of the central person in frame 3; these vehicles are behind or beside the people and are partly out of view. Across frames 1–4 the central person remains nearly centered while the left person stays left and partially occluded; by frame 5 the central person moves or turns toward the right, exposing more empty space on the left and changing the visible arm outline. This map makes object identity, overlap, and cropped boundaries clearer than RGB, but several labels and masks appear unreliable: the tie label may cover clothing or jewelry, vehicle detections are intermittent, unlabeled black regions contain visible scene structure, and mask size alone cannot provide precise distance or facing direction.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects almost no body structure in frames 1–4, so it provides little reliable information there about facing direction, gaze, limb placement, reach, or motion. In frame 5 it places a yellow upper-body skeleton on the close foreground person at the right side, showing the head above the shoulders, a bent torso/arm configuration, and magenta hand keypoints low and to the right, approximately at the camera wearer’s near-field distance and plausibly within arm’s reach. The skeleton suggests that this person is turned obliquely rather than squarely facing the camera, with the hands below the chest and partly near the lower-right image boundary; it does not establish eye gaze, and the other person and vehicles receive no pose. Compared with RGB, the map exposes an estimated joint-and-hand geometry despite dark lighting and occlusion, but the missing detections in four frames, scattered head points, overlapping hand traces, and distorted limb connections make temporal movement, exact depth, and orientation highly unreliable.
